title: Where are you from?
goal: Say where you're from, which country and city you live in, and which languages you speak — and meet the prefixes that glue straight onto the next word.
bekal: ask and answer where someone is from
say which city you live in
name the languages you speak and the one you're learning

dialogs.title: שִׂיחָה — בָּאוּלְפָּן
dialogs.intro: First day of the language course. Budi sits next to Yossi.

lines.speaker: יוֹסִי:
lines.id: Excuse me, where are you from?

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.id: And where do you live now?

lines.speaker: יוֹסִי:
lines.id: I live in Tel Aviv. And you?

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.text: גַּם אֲנִי. אֲנִי גָּר פֹּה חֹדֶשׁ.
lines.baca: gam ani. ani gar poh khodesh.
lines.id: Me too. I've been living here for a month.
lines.literal: also I. I live in-here month.

lines.speaker: יוֹסִי:
lines.id: What language do you speak at home?

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.id: Indonesian. And a little English too.

lines.speaker: יוֹסִי:
lines.text: מְעַנְיֵן! אֲנִי לֹא מַכִּיר אֶת הַשָּׂפָה הַזֹּאת.
lines.baca: me'anyen! ani lo makir et hasafah hazot.
lines.id: Interesting! I don't know that language.
lines.literal: interesting! I not know (obj) the-language the-this.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.id: You're welcome to learn it. It's easy!

notes: **מֵאַיִן אַתָּה?** (*me'ayin atah?*) is the standard "where are you from?". In everyday speech Israelis more often say **מֵאֵיפֹה אַתָּה?** (*me'eifoh atah?*) — same meaning, more casual. Both are correct; you'll hear the second one more.

⚠️ **מִ־ attaches; it never stands alone.** "From Israel" isn't two words but one: מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל. The sound shifts from *mi-* to *me-* before the throat letters (א ה ח ע ר): מֵאִינְדּוֹנֶזְיָה, מֵחֵיפָה. No need to memorize the list now — just listen, and your ear will pick it up.

**גָּר** (*gar*) means "live, reside" — not "be alive". A woman says **גָּרָה** (*garah*). This is your first verb, and it already shows a big rule of Hebrew: the verb changes form according to the gender of the subject.

**בְּ־ attaches too**: בְּתֵל אָבִיב = "in Tel Aviv". If the next word starts with הַ־ ("the"), the two prefixes merge into בַּ־: הַבַּיִת (the house) + בְּ = **בַּבַּיִת** (*babayit*, in the house). This merger comes up constantly, so learn to spot it now.

**Language names almost always end in ־ִית.** עִבְרִית (Hebrew), אַנְגְּלִית (English), אִינְדּוֹנֶזִית (Indonesian), עֲרָבִית (Arabic), רוּסִית (Russian). They're all **feminine**, so adjectives agree: עִבְרִית קַלָּה (easy Hebrew).

⚠️ **אֶת** (*et*) in line 11 has no meaning at all.** It just signals that what follows is a **definite object**. English has nothing like it, and learners forget it all the time. The easy rule: if the object has הַ־ or is a proper name, put אֶת in front of it. Covered fully in unit 7.

**רַק קְצָת** (*rak ktsat*, "only a little") is an answer you'll use for months. Learn it as a chunk. Don't answer לֹא — in Israel, being modest and then carrying on in Hebrew anyway is the fastest way to get a patient conversation partner.
**פֹּה** (*poh*) and **כָּאן** (*kan*) both mean "here" and are fully interchangeable. פֹּה is slightly more casual.

grammars.title: One-letter prefixes: Hebrew glues on what English writes separately
body: Some of the most common words in Hebrew aren't whole words but **a single letter attached** to the next word. In English these are all separate words, so your eye needs training to see them.
after: ⚠️ The practical effect is big: one Hebrew word often equals **three English words**. בַּבַּיִת = "in the house". When reading, get used to asking: "is this first letter part of the word, or a prefix?"

grammars.title: Country, nationality, language — three words from one
body: This pattern is regular and economical: from one country name you can derive the nationality (two forms) and the language.
after: Notice that **the feminine nationality and the language name are often identical** (אִינְדּוֹנֶזִית = "Indonesian woman" and "the Indonesian language"). The sentence tells them apart: אֲנִי אִינְדּוֹנֶזִית = I'm Indonesian; אֲנִי מְדַבֶּרֶת אִינְדּוֹנֶזִית = I speak Indonesian.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **אַרְצוֹת הַבְּרִית** literally means "the lands of the covenant" — that's "the United States". Israelis often shorten it to אַרְהַ"ב, pronounced *arhav*.

sections.title: Israeli cities you'll hear a lot

blocks.title: Asking with three words
items: All three use prefixes you already know: מ־ (from), an implied ב־ (in), ל־ (to). Once you see the pattern, you'll never mix them up again.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right prefix: בְּ, לְ, or מִ.
Put the words in the right order.
Write the name of the language spoken in each country.

answers: מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל — בְּחֵיפָה — לְתֵל אָבִיב — מֵאִינְדּוֹנֶזְיָה — בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם
אֲנִי מֵאִינְדּוֹנֶזְיָה. — אֲנִי גָּר בְּ... — אֲנִי מְדַבֵּר אִינְדּוֹנֶזִית. — כֵּן, קְצָת.
הִיא גָּרָה בְּתֵל אָבִיב — אֲנִי לֹא מֵאִינְדּוֹנֶזְיָה — אֲנִי מְדַבֵּר רַק קְצָת עִבְרִית — סְלִיחָה, מֵאַיִן אַתָּה?
wave: Reread the unit 1 dialogue, then add one new sentence about yourself: אֲנִי מֵ... וְאֲנִי גָּר בְּ... — say it out loud five times until you don't have to think.
